How Drill Bits Work

Why does a spiral move things when it spins?

Where shall we look?

01Which part makes the hole?↗02Where do the chips go?↗03What can we notice by turning slowly?↗04What else can a turning spiral move?↗

Which part makes the hole?

Look at the cutting edges at the tip.

A little explanation & something to try

A twist drill bit is a metal rod with spiral grooves. As it turns and moves into the material, the cutting lips at its tip shave off tiny bits called chips.

Try this. Trace the tip in the picture, then follow one spiral groove.

Where do the chips go?

Follow the chips from the bottom of the hole to the top.

A little explanation & something to try

The spiral grooves are called flutes. They help carry chips up and out as the bit turns, keeping the hole clear. The cutting lips make chips; the flutes give them a way out.

Try this. Use the diorama to follow one chip up the flute.

What can we notice by turning slowly?

Look for a curl beside the screw thread.

A little explanation & something to try

A screw has a spiral ridge called a thread. It acts like a ramp wrapped around the rod. Turning against the material helps the screw move in. A screw thread is a raised ridge; a drill flute is a groove.

Try this. With Big close by, hand-turn a screw slowly into soap or clay on a tray and look at the curls. Power drills are tools for adults; kids do not use them. Big stays close. Try turning a pencil in an enclosed hand sharpener, too.

What else can a turning spiral move?

Water rides from a low bowl to a higher cup.

A little explanation & something to try

An auger lifts loose soil or ice from a hole. An Archimedes screw lifts pockets of water along a sloping tube. A spiral slopes along its length, so turning against material can push or carry that material along. It needs something to work against, not just empty space.

Try this. Wrap a ribbon around a pencil and follow its sloping path with your eyes.

Follow the spiral

How Drill Bits Work

A spiral to follow

Little Wonderer leaned toward the magnifier. A drill bit rested on the bench. This metal rod had a spiral shape that wound around and along it. “Why all the twists?” Little asked. Big pointed to the tip. Its cutting lips are edges that shave off tiny bits of material as the bit turns.

How does the tip’s job differ from the spiral’s job?

A thread in the soap

Big slowly turned a screw into a bar of soap by hand. Little watched a pale curl gather beside it. A screw thread is a spiral ridge around a screw. As it turns against the material, the sloping thread helps pull the screw farther in. Turning can make something move along, too.

How could a sloping thread help a screw move in?

A way out for chips

Their cutaway display showed inside a hole. The drill bit’s sharp tip and cutting lips made small shavings called chips. Its spiral grooves, called flutes, gave those chips a path up and out as the bit turned. “Like a spiral slide going up!” said Little. The hole needed room for the next chips.

Why does the hole need a path for chips to leave?

A spiral in the soil

At the garden bench, Big showed Little an auger. An auger is a tool with a broad spiral for making holes in soil or ice. Its lower edge loosens material. Turning lifts the loose bits along the spiral. Little traced the path in the notebook: around, up, and out of the hole.

What do a drill bit and an auger both move out?

Water takes a ride

Back at the table, a sloping tube joined a low bowl to a high cup. Inside was an Archimedes screw, a large spiral that can lift water. Big turned its handle. Pockets of water rode up between the spiral and the tube. Little watched water reach the cup above the bowl.

How does turning help water reach a higher cup?

What else can turn?

Little found more turning tools. A corkscrew spirals into a cork to pull it out. Egg-beater gears make a hand-crank spin the beaters faster. A hand sharpener shaves pencil curls. Little drew a spiral. “Why does a spiral move things when it spins?”

Which tools move material along, and which mainly spin it?

Quiz

1. Which part of a twist drill bit shaves off material?

2. What job do the flutes do?

3. What is a screw thread?

4. What can an Archimedes screw lift?

Answer key
Quiz 1
The cutting lips at the tip shave off material as the drill bit turns.
Quiz 2
Flutes are spiral grooves that carry chips up and out of the hole.
Quiz 3
A screw thread is a spiral ridge that helps a turning screw move into material.
Quiz 4
An Archimedes screw lifts pockets of water as its spiral turns inside a sloping tube.

Small discoveries. Time together.

For grown-ups

Age 8, Grade 3 reading, Grade 2 math. Power drills are grown-up tools; kids do not use them. A grown-up stays close and leads the soap or clay activity, placing the material on a tray and choosing the screw. Use an enclosed hand pencil sharpener for the pencil-curl observation. The illustrated drill bit is a common twist bit. Its cutting lips remove material; flutes provide chip clearance as the bit rotates and advances. The diorama isolates chip travel in a fixed cutaway, with enlarged chips and a shortened path. Real chip shapes and motion depend on the material and bit. Screw threads are raised ridges, unlike the recessed flutes. A turning spiral needs contact or confinement to move material along. The egg beater uses gears for faster rotation; it does not lift material like an auger.

Age 8 / Grade 3 reading. Welcome spoken answers and dictation. Use the story to explain drill bit, spiral, flute, cutting lip, chips, screw thread, and auger.

About the pictures and numbers. Pictures are imagined, enlarged illustrations, not photographs or measurements. Math numbers are made up for the story.

Illustration explanations: Sandvik Coromant · drill flutes and chip removal · Science Buddies · the Archimedes screw
